title: How Shaped Waves Propagate in Scattering Media
abstract: The radiative transport equation provides a powerful framework for describing wave propagation in scattering media. However, it cannot describe coherent waves whose incident wavefront is deliberately tailored. Here we establish a transport theory for wavefront-controlled waves based on a matrix transport equation. Unlike conventional radiative transport, which propagates a scalar radiance, our theory propagates a complex two-by-two matrix that retains phase information and obeys a nonlinear transport equation, despite the underlying wave dynamics being linear. We use this matrix transport equation to derive the spatial profiles of the energy and current densities of transmission eigenchannels, from closed to open channels, in arbitrary diffusive systems. Remarkably, these profiles can be expressed analytically in terms of the solution of the conventional radiative transport equation for a random wave in the same medium. The theory further extends to energy loss, including absorption and leakage into uncontrolled channels, revealing symmetry breaking of transmission eigenchannels in complex structures. Validated against numerical solutions of the wave equation, we establish matrix transport as a framework for describing and controlling coherent wave propagation in complex media.
summary: This work introduces a Matrix Transport Equation (MTE) to describe coherent wave propagation in scattering media, overcoming the limitations of standard radiative transport theory. The MTE tracks phase information via a complex matrix, allowing for the derivation of analytical profiles for shaped wave channels. This framework provides a powerful tool for controlling wave energy in complex, disordered structures.
main_problem: The paper develops a transport theory for wave propagation in scattering media when the incident wavefront is deliberately shaped, a regime beyond the scope of conventional radiative transport equations.
main_result: A matrix transport equation (MTE) is established that governs coherent wave propagation, yielding analytical expressions for energy and current densities of transmission eigenchannels.
method: The theory uses a complex two-by-two matrix transport equation (MTE) that propagates phase information, contrasting it with the scalar radiance used in the standard Radiative Transport Equation (RTE).
model_or_system: The system models wave propagation in scattering media, analyzed using the MTE. The theory is applied to characterize transmission eigenchannels in disordered waveguides and slabs.
key_observables: Transmission eigenchannel intensity profiles ($I_T(\mathbf{r})$), transmission eigenvalue distribution ($ho(T)$), and the matrix radiance ($g(u, \mathbf{r})$).
important_parameters: The degree of disorder, the mean transmission ($ ar{T}$), and the boundary conditions of the scattering region.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the MTE is necessary when wavefront shaping occurs, and the theory can be extended to include absorption and leakage.
figures_summary: Figures compare plane wave propagation (RTE regime) versus shaped wave propagation (MTE regime), and show the derived intensity profiles ($I_T(r)$) against classical diffusion predictions ($ ar{I}(r)$).
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the MTE as an extension to the RTE, derives the analytic forms for eigenchannel profiles, and then analyzes the distribution of transmission eigenvalues ($ho(T)$) in both lossless and lossy regimes, concluding with numerical validation using alternative parametrizations.
why_interesting: The development of a matrix transport theory that retains phase information is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics, providing a framework to control wave dynamics beyond simple diffusive approximations.

In a lossless waveguide, Eq. (3) admits a solution for Q(r) confined to a great circle connecting Qin and Qout (red curve), orthogonal to all the spatial components of the matrix current J(r), the latter being collinear in matrix space. In the presence of loss, the trajectory of Q(r) depends on the path followed (green curves) but remains constrained to the sphere (see Supplementary Sec. D). In this case, the spatial components of J(r) are not collinear in general.
